This will be my interpretation of the merits and drawbacks of veganism and keto, and a comparison of the two. While I'll do my best to be unbiased, be warned, if you are a proponent of either one, you may want to look away. Unless you just like getting angry, then by all means, continue.

Today I'll be comparing two fringe diets, veganism, and keto. I'll discuss what each of them are, what each of them do, and what effects you can expect from each. First off, let's define them.

In this article, "veganism" will be defined as "a diet using no animal food sources", and "keto" will be defined as "a diet using fat as such a large portion of the diet that it is used as a primary fuel source rather than carbohydrates". While I can find no official dictionary of fitness terms to source this from, those, as far as I can tell, are the common-use definitions.

Now let's go into the claims of each. While they are nutritionally about as different as two diets can be, in terms of claims, veganism and keto are very similar. For starters, proponents of both diets claim that their style of eating is just as anabolic as a traditional bodybuilding diet. Secondly, and another big one, is that proponents of each claim that their respective diet has anti-cancer properties. Thirdly, proponents of each often recommend their diet specifically for weight loss. Though I'm sure I could find more claims that are common between the two, let's run with those three for now.

So, can veganism, or keto, build muscle as well as a traditional bodybuilding diet? Let's first consider protein. While there are numerous recommendations out there for protein consumption levels, and almost as many studies backing up and debunking each other, a common and moderate suggestion is 1 gram per pound of lean body mass per day. Let's go with that.

Can you consume enough protein with either diet to meet this recommendation? Sure, but there are complications. First, let's start with keto. The maximum amount of protein you can consume and stay in ketosis is about 20% of your caloric intake. For someone with 160lbs of lean body mass, this means that your total daily caloric intake would have to be about 3200 calories, there being 4 calories in a gram of protein. This means, at least for most people with roughly 160lbs of lean body mass, that they would need to be either bulking, or doing a good amount of cardio, or both, to be able to get in the recommended amount of protein while staying in ketosis.

Veganism is similar in this regard. Without use of protein powder, you would need to be taking in a very large number of calories to meet the protein requirement, due to the relatively low protein density of naturally occurring plant foods. Protein powder, it might seem at first glance, solves this problem. Just chug a few vegan protein shakes daily and you're there! Well, it's not that simple. Due to things like protein quality, bioavailabilty, and amino acid profile, plant protein don't quite measure up to animal proteins in terms of muscle building abilities. Even for something like soy protein concentrate, one of the more complete and dense plant protein sources, roughly twice as many calories need to be eaten to get the same amount of usable protein as in chicken breast. [To see more on this highly complicated topic, as well as use a cool calculator that lets you compare plant sources with chicken breast, I recommend checking out this page.] So, the takeaway is that veganism, like keto, makes it a struggle to obtain optimum amounts of protein, and that either bulking or tons of cardio would need to be done to make it work. [Note that building muscle with sub-optimal levels of protein IS possible, it will just occur at a correspondingly sub-optimal rate].

Next, let's check out the claims that either diet has some kind of cancer preventative properties. I'm sure this is a touchy topic and I freely admit that I am not a doctor. However, most of these veganism/keto people aren't doctors either. Keep that in mind.

Veganism seems to base it's assertion that it is anti-cancer on a few studies showing a weak correlation between veganism and cancer prevention, and the idea that meat contains unspecified "toxins" that are cancer-causing. The studies tend to show a 5-10% increased rate of certain types of cancers in meat eaters, as opposed to vegans [see here and here]. However, let's not forget that correlations /= causation, and that it may very well be that vegans in general are more aware of their eating habits than omnivores, and thus cut out highly-processed foods, that are more likely cancer suspects than simple meat.

Keto bases it's supposed anti-cancer properties on the fact that cancer cells need glucose to survive, and that keto removes glucose as the main fuel source of the body. While some glucose is still produced internally, the thought process is that keto starves the cancer cells of fuel and they die. To me, it seems like keto already has a stronger anti-cancer claim than veganism, having at least a proposed mechanism other than just "toxins". However, it doesn't seem that any large-scale studies have been done, although a promising few small ones have. For a very thorough and skeptical overview of the matter, I recommend checking this page out.

Now for fat burning. The short of the thing is, yes. They can both burn fat. Any diet that has you eat less calories than you use can burn fat. I suspect that many of the fanatical proponents of both of these diets are ex-fatties who were finally pushed away from the SAD [standard American diet] by their chosen one. Naturally they lose fat, and their view of either diet as the ultimate one was cemented.

Finally, what are some of the disadvantages of either diet? For keto, the big one I can think of is that any anaerobic exercise you do, your anaerobic system needing glucose for fuel, will utterly suck. Your sprints will be slower, your jumps will be shorter, and your strength will go down, or stagnate, or at least not improve as fast as it could. Sorry, that's the problem with removing the main fuel source of your anaerobic energy system. Veganism's main disadvantage is how easy it will be to slip into deficiency of so many vitamins and minerals. B12, for example, is basically impossible to get on a vegan diet, and omega-3s from plant sources are poorly absorbed. Thus, supplementation will be a must.

TL;DR- neither diet is great for muscle building, although it can be done, a traditional bodybuilding diet would be easier and better. Both diets have weak claims against cancer. Either diet can help you lose fat, but so can any other low calorie diet. Furthermore, both diets have large drawbacks that subtract from their small advantages so much that they are both solidly in the negative. Avoid if you have good sense.
